key_terms.meaning: T{a x₁ + b x₂} = a y₁ + b y₂ for all inputs and constants: additivity plus homogeneity.
If x(t) → y(t), then x(t−t₀) → y(t−t₀) for every delay t₀.
Output for input δ(t), system at rest. RC low-pass: h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t).
Output for input u(t); s(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>t</sup>h(λ)dλ and h(t)=ds/dt.
y(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ; for causal h and x starting at 0, limits 0 to t.
Graphical convolution: flip h(τ) to h(−τ), slide to h(t−τ), multiply by x(τ), integrate over the overlap.
Start times add and end times add, so T<sub>y</sub>=T<sub>x</sub>+T<sub>h</sub> for finite-width signals; area(y)=area(x)·area(h).
Causal LTI system ⇔ h(t)=0 for t<0.
Σ a<sub>k</sub> d<sup>k</sup>y/dt<sup>k</sup> = Σ b<sub>k</sub> d<sup>k</sup>x/dt<sup>k</sup> with constant a<sub>k</sub>, b<sub>k</sub>; RC circuit: RC dy/dt+y=x, τ=RC.
y=y<sub>n</sub>+y<sub>f</sub>: y<sub>n</sub> from the characteristic roots, y<sub>f</sub> shaped like the input.
Total = response to stored energy alone + response to input alone from rest (x*h).
x′=Ax+Bu, y=Cx+Du; n states for an nth-order system.
x₁=y, x₂=y′, …; last row of A is −a₀, −a₁, …; with u′ on the right use x₂=y′−b₁u.

takeaways: An LTI system obeys superposition and time invariance; test each with two paths, and one mismatch is enough to fail.
Because every input is an integral of shifted impulses, the impulse response h(t) fixes the output for every input.
The step response is the running integral of h(t), and h(t) is its slope; a jump in s(t) is an impulse in h(t).
Convolution y=x*h is evaluated by flip, slide, multiply and integrate over the overlap, with a separate case between each pair of breakpoints.
Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive with δ(t) as identity: cascades multiply into h₁*h₂, parallel branches add into h₁+h₂.
Causality is a condition on where h(t) lives (zero for t<0); BIBO stability is a condition on its absolute area. Neither implies the other.
A linear constant-coefficient differential equation is an LTI system from rest; its solution splits into natural plus forced, or zero-input plus zero-state.
An nth-order differential equation becomes n first-order state equations x′=Ax+Bu, y=Cx+Du, which computers integrate directly.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a convolution worked graphically or analytically, the step response from h(t) or from a differential equation, a causality and stability test on h(t), and a proof that an LTI system is fixed by its impulse response. Every long question below has the points an examiner looks for and a full model answer.

bank.q: Define a continuous-time LTI system. Explain the superposition and time-invariance properties, and show why an LTI system is fully characterised by its impulse response.
outline: Definition of linearity: additivity and homogeneity
Definition of time invariance with a shifted input
Input written as an integral of shifted impulses
Impulse response as the response to δ(t)
Output as the convolution of the input with h(t)
answer: System. A continuous-time system maps an input x(t) to an output y(t)=T{x(t)}, with t in seconds. It is LTI when it is both linear and time-invariant.

answer.text: Linearity (superposition). For all inputs x₁, x₂ and all constants a, b:
answer.pre: T{a x₁(t) + b x₂(t)} = a T{x₁(t)} + b T{x₂(t)} = a y₁(t) + b y₂(t)

answer: Superposition combines two properties: additivity (a=b=1: the response to a sum is the sum of responses) and homogeneity (b=0: scaling the input scales the output). Putting a=b=0 gives T{0}=0, so a linear system gives zero output for zero input. This is necessary but not sufficient.

answer.text: Time invariance. A delay of the input by any t₀ delays the output by the same t₀; the rule does not depend on clock time:
answer.pre: if x(t) → y(t), then x(t − t₀) → y(t − t₀) for every t₀

answer.text: Testing the two properties on y(t)=3x(t)+2. Linearity with x₁=1, x₂=2, a=2, b=3: combining first gives T{8}=26; applying T separately gives 2(5)+3(8)=34. 26≠34, so the system is not linear. Time invariance with x(t)=t, t₀=2 s: both paths give 3t−4, which is 11 at t=5 s, so the system is time-invariant. It is not LTI.

answer: Impulse response. h(t) is the output when the input is the unit impulse δ(t) and the system starts at rest.

answer.text: Input as impulses. By the sifting property, any input is an integral of shifted, weighted impulses, with τ a dummy variable along the input's time axis:
answer.pre: x(t) = ∫ x(τ) δ(t − τ) dτ,   τ from −∞ to ∞

answer: Apply the two properties. Time invariance: δ(t−τ) gives h(t−τ). Homogeneity: the weighted impulse x(τ)dτ·δ(t−τ) gives x(τ)dτ·h(t−τ). Additivity: the response to the whole integral is the integral of the responses.

answer.text: Result.
answer.pre: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ = x(t) * h(t),   τ from −∞ to ∞

answer: Conclusion. Once h(t) is known, the convolution integral gives the output for every input, so h(t) characterises the system completely. Causality and stability can also be read from h(t). This needs both properties: for a non-LTI system the response to δ(t−τ) is not a shifted copy of one signal, and responses cannot be added.

Why both properties are needed. Take the linear but time-varying system y(t)=t·x(t). Its response to δ(t−τ) is t·δ(t−τ)=τ·δ(t−τ), which is not a shifted copy of its response to δ(t) (that response is 0·δ(t)=0). So no single h(t) describes it, and the convolution integral does not apply. Linearity alone lets responses be added; time invariance makes every response a shifted copy of the same h.

What else h(t) gives. Because h(t) fixes the system, every other property can be read from it: memoryless if h=Kδ(t); causal if h=0 for t<0; BIBO stable if ∫|h|dt is finite; the frequency response H(jω) and transfer function H(s) are its Fourier and Laplace transforms, treated in Fourier analysis and Laplace transform analysis.

Closing check with numbers. An RC filter with R=1 kΩ, C=1 μF has h(t)=1000e−1000tu(t) s−1. For x(t)=u(t), y(t)=∫0t1000e−1000(t−τ)dτ=1−e−1000t for t≥0, so y(1 ms)=1−e−1=0.632 V for a 1 V step: exactly the capacitor voltage that the circuit's own equation gives.

bank.q: Define the impulse response h(t) and the step response s(t) of a continuous-time LTI system. Derive the relations s(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>t</sup>h(λ)dλ and h(t)=ds(t)/dt.
outline: Definitions with the system initially at rest
Step response as the convolution of u(t) with h(t)
Jumps in s(t) give impulses in h(t)
answer: Impulse response. h(t) is the output of the LTI system when the input is δ(t), with no energy stored at the start.
Step response. s(t) is the output when the input is the unit step u(t), again from rest. Some books call it the indicial response.

answer.text: Step response by convolution. The output for any input is the convolution of the input with h. For x=u, using the commutative form and λ as the dummy variable:
answer.pre: s(t) = ∫ h(λ) u(t − λ) dλ,   λ from −∞ to ∞

answer.text: Limits. u(t−λ)=1 when t−λ≥0, that is when λ≤t, and 0 when λ>t. So the integrand is h(λ) up to λ=t and zero beyond:
answer.pre: s(t) = ∫ h(λ) dλ,   λ from −∞ to t

answer: For a causal system h(λ)=0 for λ<0, so the lower limit becomes 0: s(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>h(λ)dλ for t≥0 and s(t)=0 for t<0.

Derivative relation. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, differentiating an integral with respect to its upper limit gives the integrand at that limit: h(t)=ds(t)/dt. The same result follows from u′(t)=δ(t): differentiating the input differentiates the output of an LTI system.
Jumps. If s(t) jumps by J at an instant, ds/dt contains J·δ at that instant. A step response that rises smoothly from zero gives an h with no impulse.

answer.text: Example 1 (smooth rise). RC filter, τ=1 ms: h(t)=1000e−1000tu(t) s−1.
answer.pre:
s(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 1000 e<sup>−1000λ</sup> dλ = 1 − e<sup>−1000t</sup>,   t ≥ 0
ds/dt = 1000 e<sup>−1000t</sup> = h(t)   ✓

answer.text: Example 2 (jump). s(t)=(1−0.5e−2t)u(t). At t=0 it jumps from 0 to 0.5, so h has 0.5δ(t). For t>0, ds/dt=e−2t. Hence h(t)=0.5δ(t)+e−2tu(t).

answer: Second derivation, from superposition. Without convolution: u(t) is the running integral of δ(t). Integration is itself an LTI operation, and two LTI operations in cascade can be applied in either order (associative and commutative laws). So integrating the input first or the output afterwards gives the same result: the response to the integral of δ, which is s, equals the integral of the response to δ, which is ∫h.

Why engineers use the relation. A step is easy to apply in a laboratory (close a switch), while a true impulse is not. So s(t) is measured and h(t) is obtained as its slope. The final value s(∞) is the DC gain of the system.

answer.text: Values for example 1. The slope of s equals h at every instant:

answer: Mistakes that cost marks. Writing s=dh/dt instead of h=ds/dt gives, for the RC filter, s=−106e−1000t, a large negative number for a capacitor that charges upward. Dropping the lower limit's meaning (integrating from −∞ for a causal h but forgetting h=0 there) changes nothing numerically, but writing ∫0∞ instead of ∫0t gives the constant 1 for every t, which is the final value, not the response.
Closing check. The final value of s must equal the total area of h. Example 1: area=1000×(1/1000)=1=s(∞). Example 2: 0.5 (impulse) + ∫0∞e−2tdt=0.5+0.5=1=s(∞). Both relations hold.

bank.q: State the commutative, associative, distributive and identity properties of continuous-time convolution. Give one system-level meaning of each property.
outline: Identity x*δ=x and the shift x*δ(t−t₀)
answer: Notation. x*h means ∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ over all τ, where τ is the dummy variable and t the output time.

answer.text: Commutative. x*h=h*x. Proof: put λ=t−τ, so dτ=−dλ and the limits swap; the integral becomes ∫h(λ)x(t−λ)dλ.
answer.pre: ∫ x(τ) h(t−τ) dτ  =  ∫ h(λ) x(t−λ) dλ

answer: System meaning: the roles of input and impulse response can be exchanged. A system with impulse response h driven by x gives the same output as a system with impulse response x driven by h. In practice you flip whichever signal is simpler.

Associative. (x*h₁)*h₂=x*(h₁*h₂). Proof: write the double integral and swap the order of integration. System meaning: two LTI systems in cascade equal one system with impulse response h₁*h₂; together with commutativity, the order of the two blocks does not matter.

Distributive. x*(h₁+h₂)=x*h₁+x*h₂. Proof: the integral of a sum is the sum of integrals. System meaning: two LTI systems fed by the same input, with their outputs added, equal one system with impulse response h₁+h₂.
Identity. x*δ=x, because ∫x(τ)δ(t−τ)dτ picks out x(t) (sifting). More generally x(t)*δ(t−t₀)=x(t−t₀). System meaning: h(t)=δ(t) is a plain wire, and h(t)=δ(t−t₀) is an ideal delay of t₀ seconds.

answer.text: Worked check of associativity (cascade). Let h₁(t)=e−tu(t) and h₂(t)=e−2tu(t). For t≥0:
answer.pre:
h₁*h₂ = ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>−τ</sup> e<sup>−2(t−τ)</sup> dτ = e<sup>−2t</sup> ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>τ</sup> dτ = e<sup>−2t</sup>(e<sup>t</sup> − 1)
      = (e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>) u(t)

answer: So the cascade acts as one system with h(t)=(e<sup>−t</sup>−e<sup>−2t</sup>)u(t). Swapping the blocks gives h₂*h₁, which by commutativity is the same signal.

answer.text: Associativity in detail. Writing out both sides as double integrals:
answer.pre:
[(x*h₁)*h₂](t) = ∫∫ x(σ) h₁(τ−σ) h₂(t−τ) dσ dτ
put τ = σ + λ:  = ∫ x(σ) [ ∫ h₁(λ) h₂(t−σ−λ) dλ ] dσ = [x*(h₁*h₂)](t)

answer: Distributive law with numbers. A wire (δ(t)) in parallel with a first-order lag (e−tu(t)) has h=δ(t)+e−tu(t). Its step response is the sum of the two step responses: u(t)+(1−e−t)u(t). At t=1 s this is 1+0.632=1.632.
Identity and shift with numbers. x(t)=e−tu(t) convolved with δ(t−2) gives e−(t−2)u(t−2): the same curve starting 2 s later, so its value at t=3 s is e−1=0.368, the value x had at t=1 s.

Mistakes that cost marks. Claiming the laws hold for every system: they hold for convolution, so the system-level meanings need LTI blocks. Two nonlinear blocks in cascade cannot be swapped: squaring then adding 1 gives x²+1, while adding 1 then squaring gives (x+1)². Writing x*δ=0 (as if δ were zero almost everywhere) instead of x*δ=x.

answer.text: Closing check with numbers. The area of a convolution is the product of the areas. Area of h₁=1, area of h₂=1/2, product 0.5. Area of the cascade: ∫0∞(e−t−e−2t)dt=1−0.5=0.5. They agree. For two unit rectangles of widths 2 s and 3 s the same check gives 2×3=6, the area of their 5 s trapezoid.

Formula

bank.q: Define causality and BIBO stability for a continuous-time LTI system. State the necessary and sufficient conditions on h(t) for each, and justify them.
outline: Causal: output depends only on present and past input
BIBO: every bounded input gives a bounded output
answer: Causality. A system is causal if the output at any time t depends only on the input at times up to t, never on future input.

answer.text: Condition. Write the output in the commutative form:
answer.pre: y(t) = ∫ h(τ) x(t − τ) dτ,   τ from −∞ to ∞

answer: The weight h(τ) multiplies the input at time t−τ. For τ<0, t−τ>t lies in the future. The output is free of future input for every x only if all these weights vanish. So an LTI system is causal if and only if h(t)=0 for t<0. h(0) may be nonzero.
BIBO stability. A system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every input with |x(t)|≤Mx<∞ for all t gives an output with |y(t)|≤My<∞ for all t.

answer.text: Condition. An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if h(t) is absolutely integrable:
answer.pre: ∫ |h(t)| dt < ∞,   t from −∞ to ∞

answer.text: Sufficiency. If the area S=∫|h|dt is finite and |x|≤Mx:
answer.pre: |y(t)| ≤ ∫ |h(τ)| |x(t−τ)| dτ ≤ M<sub>x</sub> ∫ |h(τ)| dτ = M<sub>x</sub> · S

answer: So every output is bounded by M<sub>x</sub>·S.

Necessity. Suppose S is infinite. Choose the bounded input x(t)=sgn[h(−t)], equal to +1, −1 or 0. Then y(0)=∫h(τ)x(−τ)dτ=∫h(τ)sgn[h(τ)]dτ=∫|h(τ)|dτ=∞. A bounded input has produced an unbounded output, so the system is not stable.

answer.text: Examples.

answer: Independence. The table shows that neither property implies the other: one is about where h lives, the other about how much absolute area it has.

Examples of the causality test. e−2tu(t) and δ(t−1) are zero before t=0, so causal. u(t+1) switches on at t=−1 s, so noncausal. A smoothing filter that averages x over t−1 to t+1 has h=0.5 on −1≤t≤1, so it uses future input and is noncausal; it is still usable offline on stored data.

Examples of the stability test. e−2|t| has area 2×(1/2)=1, so it is stable although noncausal. The ideal low-pass impulse response sin(t)/(πt) has net area 1 but infinite absolute area, so it is not BIBO stable: the absolute value in the test matters.

How to answer in an exam. State each definition, state each condition on h(t), give the one-line sufficiency bound and the sgn[h(−t)] input for necessity, then test one causal-stable and one causal-unstable example to show the properties are independent.

Mistakes that cost marks. Stating the stability test without the absolute value; claiming causal implies stable (u(t) is a counterexample); using h(0)=0 as part of the causality condition (δ(t) itself is causal); and testing stability with one bounded input, which proves nothing: the condition is on h(t).

Closing check with numbers. For h(t)=e−2tu(t) and an input bounded by 5 V, the output is bounded by 5×0.5=2.5 V. The constant input x=5 V (for all t) gives y=5∫0∞e−2τdτ=2.5 V, which reaches the bound, so the bound is tight.

bank.q: Let x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) and h(t)=u(t)−u(t−3), t in seconds. Evaluate y(t)=x(t)*h(t) by the convolution integral and give y(t) for all t.
outline: Find where x(τ) and h(t−τ) are nonzero
Integrate the exponential in each case
State the piecewise result and check continuity and area

answer.text: Set up.
answer.pre: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ,   τ from −∞ to ∞

answer: Where each factor is nonzero. x(τ)=e−2τ for τ≥0. h(t−τ)=1 when 0≤t−τ<3, that is when t−3<τ≤t: a window of width 3 s whose right edge sits at τ=t.
Breakpoints. The window's right edge meets the start of x at t=0, and its left edge t−3 passes τ=0 at t=3. So the cases are t<0, 0≤t<3 and t≥3.
Case t<0. The whole window lies at negative τ, where x=0. y(t)=0.

answer.text: Case 0≤t<3. The window covers 0≤τ≤t of the input:
answer.pre: y(t) = ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>−2τ</sup> dτ = [−e<sup>−2τ</sup>/2]₀ᵗ = (1 − e<sup>−2t</sup>)/2

answer.text: Case t≥3. The window covers t−3≤τ≤t, all at positive τ:
answer.pre:
y(t) = ∫ from (t−3) to t of e<sup>−2τ</sup> dτ = [−e<sup>−2τ</sup>/2] from (t−3) to t
     = (e<sup>−2(t−3)</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>)/2 = e<sup>−2t</sup>(e<sup>6</sup> − 1)/2

answer.text: Result.
Values. The output rises while more of the input enters the window, peaks at t=3 s and then decays as the window slides past the large early values of x.

answer: Continuity at t=3. The first case gives (1−e−6)/2=0.4988; the second gives (e0−e−6)/2=0.4988. They join, as they must since neither signal has an impulse.

Meaning. h(t) is a 3 s moving integrator: y(t) is the area of x over the last 3 seconds. Early on that area grows towards the full area 1/2 of x; after t=3 s the early part of x drops out of the window.

Picture of each case. For 0≤t<3 the window has entered the input from the left and covers all of x up to τ=t. For t≥3 the window has a left edge t−3>0, so it has dropped the oldest part of x, which was also the largest part.

answer.text: Cross-check with the properties. h(t)=u(t)−u(t−3) is a step minus a delayed step. By the distributive and shift laws, y(t)=r(t)−r(t−3), where r(t) is the response to u(t), that is the running integral of x:
answer.pre:
r(t) = ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>−2τ</sup> dτ = ½(1 − e<sup>−2t</sup>) u(t)
y(4) = r(4) − r(1) = ½(1 − e<sup>−8</sup>) − ½(1 − e<sup>−2</sup>) = ½(e<sup>−2</sup> − e<sup>−8</sup>) = 0.068

answer: This matches the table value y(4)=0.068, and for t<3 the term r(t−3) is zero, so y=r(t), matching the first case.

Common mistakes. Using 0 to t as limits for t≥3 gives (1−e−2t)/2, which tends to 0.5 instead of decaying to 0; a 3 s window cannot keep the whole input forever. Writing h(t−τ)=1 on 0≤τ≤3 forgets that the window moves with t.

answer.text: Second route: flip x instead of h. By commutativity y=∫h(τ)x(t−τ)dτ. Now h(τ)=1 on 0≤τ<3 and x(t−τ)=e−2(t−τ) for τ≤t:
answer.pre:
0 ≤ t < 3:  y = ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>−2(t−τ)</sup> dτ = ½(1 − e<sup>−2t</sup>)
t ≥ 3:      y = ∫₀³ e<sup>−2(t−τ)</sup> dτ = ½e<sup>−2t</sup>(e<sup>6</sup> − 1)

answer: Both routes give the same pieces, as the commutative law requires. Flipping the rectangle is usually easier, because its flipped copy has the same shape.

Closing check. The area of y must be area(x)×area(h)=(1/2)×3=1.5. Integrating the two pieces: ∫03(1−e−2t)/2 dt=1.5−0.25(1−e−6)=1.2506 and ∫3∞(e6−1)e−2t/2 dt=(1−e−6)/4=0.2494. Sum 1.5000. The answer is consistent.

bank.q: An LTI system has h(t)=e<sup>−at</sup>u(t) with a>0. Find its step response using the convolution integral, and verify the result by differentiating it. Evaluate for a=2 s<sup>−1</sup>.
outline: Differentiate to recover h(t), including the jump term

answer.text: Set up. The step response is the output for x(t)=u(t). Using the commutative form:
answer.pre: s(t) = ∫ h(τ) u(t − τ) dτ,   τ from −∞ to ∞

answer: Nonzero ranges. h(τ)=e−aτ for τ≥0 and 0 for τ<0. u(t−τ)=1 for τ≤t and 0 for τ>t. Both are nonzero on 0≤τ≤t, which exists only when t≥0.
Case t<0. No overlap, so s(t)=0.

answer.text: Case t≥0.
answer.pre: s(t) = ∫₀ᵗ e<sup>−aτ</sup> dτ = [−e<sup>−aτ</sup>/a]₀ᵗ = (1/a)(1 − e<sup>−at</sup>)

answer: Result. s(t)=(1/a)(1−e−at)u(t).

answer.text: Verify by differentiating. Use the product rule on (1/a)(1−e−at)·u(t), with du/dt=δ(t):
answer.pre:
ds/dt = (1/a)(a e<sup>−at</sup>) u(t) + (1/a)(1 − e<sup>−at</sup>) δ(t)
      = e<sup>−at</sup> u(t) + (1/a)(1 − 1) δ(t)        (δ(t) samples the bracket at t = 0)
      = e<sup>−at</sup> u(t) = h(t)   ✓

answer: The impulse term vanishes because s(t) is continuous at t=0 (it starts from 0), so h contains no impulse.
Initial and final values. s(0)=(1/a)(1−1)=0: the output starts from rest. s(∞)=1/a, which equals ∫0∞e−atdt=1/a, the area of h (the DC gain).

answer.text: Numbers for a=2 s−1. s(t)=0.5(1−e−2t)u(t).

answer: Time constant view. h(t)=e−atu(t) is an RC-type system with τ=1/a=0.5 s and DC gain 1/a. At t=τ=0.5 s, s reaches 0.632 of its final value: 0.632×0.5=0.316, matching the table.

answer.text: Check with the differential equation. h(t)=e−atu(t) is the impulse response of dy/dt+ay=x. For a unit step and t>0:
answer.pre: ds/dt + a s = e<sup>−at</sup> + (1 − e<sup>−at</sup>) = 1 = x   ✓,   s(0) = 0   ✓

answer: The role of a. 1/a is the time constant. Larger a gives a faster but smaller response (final value 1/a). For a=10 s−1: s settles at 0.1 within about 0.5 s. For a=0.5 s−1: s settles at 2 after about 10 s.
If a were negative. For a=−1 the same formula gives s(t)=et−1, which is 19.1 at t=3 s and keeps growing: h=etu(t) has infinite area, so the system is unstable. This is why the question says a>0.
Sketch. h starts at 1 and decays to 0; s starts at 0 with slope 1, bends over and levels off at 1/a. The area under h up to time t is exactly the height of s at t.

Mistakes that cost marks. Dropping the 1/a: s=1−e−2t gives s(1)=0.865 instead of 0.432 for a=2, and a final value of 1 instead of 0.5, which no longer equals the area of h. Integrating from 0 to ∞ instead of 0 to t gives the constant 1/a. Forgetting u(t) in the answer suggests a nonzero output before the step is applied.

Closing check. A numerical slope from the table: [s(1)−s(0.5)]/0.5=(0.432−0.316)/0.5=0.232, which lies between h(0.5)=0.368 and h(1)=0.135, as the slope of a curve whose slope falls from 0.368 to 0.135 must.

bank.q: A system is described by dy(t)/dt+3y(t)=2x(t). Find its impulse response h(t) and step response s(t) by time-domain reasoning, and check both.
outline: Solve the homogeneous equation for t>0
Find y(0⁺) by integrating the equation across t=0
Check in the differential equation and the final value
answer: Plan. h(t) is the response to x=δ(t) with the system at rest, y(0−)=0. For t>0 the input is zero, so h is a natural response; the impulse only sets its starting value.
Natural response. With x=0, dy/dt+3y=0. The characteristic equation λ+3=0 gives λ=−3 s−1, so for t>0, h(t)=Ae−3t.

answer.text: Starting value. Integrate the equation with x=δ(t) from t=0− to t=0+:
answer.pre: y(0<sup>+</sup>) − y(0<sup>−</sup>) + 3 ∫ y dt = 2 ∫ δ(t) dt      (integrals from 0<sup>−</sup> to 0<sup>+</sup>)

answer: y has no impulse (otherwise dy/dt would contain δ′, which the right side lacks), so ∫y dt over a zero-width interval is 0. The right side is 2. With y(0<sup>−</sup>)=0 this gives y(0<sup>+</sup>)=2, so A=2.
Impulse response. h(t)=2e−3tu(t). The system is causal (zero before t=0) and stable (area 2/3).

answer.text: Check h in the equation. Differentiate with the product rule, using u′=δ:
answer.pre:
dh/dt = −6 e<sup>−3t</sup> u(t) + 2 e<sup>0</sup> δ(t) = −6 e<sup>−3t</sup> u(t) + 2 δ(t)
dh/dt + 3h = −6 e<sup>−3t</sup> u(t) + 2 δ(t) + 6 e<sup>−3t</sup> u(t) = 2 δ(t)   ✓

answer.text: Step response. s is the running integral of h:
answer.pre: s(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 2 e<sup>−3λ</sup> dλ = (2/3)(1 − e<sup>−3t</sup>),   t ≥ 0

answer: Check s directly. With x=u(t), for t>0: ds/dt+3s=2e−3t+2−2e−3t=2=2x ✓. And s(0)=0, as it must be from rest.

answer.text: Final value check. At steady state dy/dt=0, so 3y=2x and the DC gain is 2/3. s(∞)=2/3 and the area of h, ∫0∞2e−3tdt=2/3, agree.

answer: Second method: step response first. Solve with x=u(t): forced response yf=2/3 (from 3y=2), natural response Ae−3t. From rest y(0)=0, so A=−2/3 and s(t)=(2/3)(1−e−3t)u(t). Differentiate: h=ds/dt=2e−3tu(t), plus (2/3)(1−1)δ(t)=0. Both methods agree.

Why y(0+)=2 makes sense. The equation says dy/dt=2x−3y. An impulse of area 1 in x adds 2 to the integral of dy/dt across t=0, so y jumps from 0 to 2. After that the input is zero and y decays with time constant 1/3 s.
Units. If x and y are voltages, h has unit s−1, and h(0+)=2 s−1. s is dimensionless per volt of step: a 1 V step gives a final output of 0.667 V.

Mistakes that cost marks. Taking y(0+)=1 instead of 2 (ignoring the coefficient of x) gives h=e−3tu(t) and a final step value of 0.333 instead of 0.667, which disagrees with the steady-state equation 3y=2x. Writing h=2e−3t without u(t) claims a response before the impulse. Using s(0)=2 (the impulse's starting value) for the step response instead of s(0)=0.
Sketch. h jumps to 2 at t=0+ and decays, falling to 2e−1=0.736 at t=1/3 s. s starts at 0 with slope 2 (equal to h(0+)), bends over and levels off at 2/3; at t=1/3 s it is 0.421.
Closing check. The time constant is 1/3 s. At t=1/3 s, s should be 0.632 of 2/3: (2/3)(1−e−1)=0.421. The table's s(0.5)=0.518 is past that point and below 0.667, as expected.

bank.q: For h(t)=e<sup>−4t</sup>u(t), test causality and BIBO stability. Compute the area ∫|h(t)|dt and the bound on the output for an input bounded by 8 V.
outline: No conflict between the two properties
answer: Causality. u(t)=0 for t<0, so h(t)=0 for t<0. The condition for a causal LTI system holds: the system is causal. (h(0)=1 is allowed; only negative time is ruled out.)

answer.text: Area under |h|. h(t)≥0 everywhere, so |h(t)|=h(t):
answer.pre: ∫ |h(t)| dt = ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−4t</sup> dt = [−e<sup>−4t</sup>/4]₀<sup>∞</sup> = 0 − (−1/4) = 1/4

answer: Stability. The area is finite (0.25), so h is absolutely integrable and the system is BIBO stable.

answer.text: Output bound. For |x(t)|≤Mx:
answer.pre: |y(t)| ≤ M<sub>x</sub> ∫ |h(τ)| dτ = M<sub>x</sub> × 0.25

answer: With M<sub>x</sub>=8 V the output can never exceed 8×0.25=2 V in magnitude, whatever the shape of the input.
The bound is reached. A constant input x(t)=8 V for all t gives y=8∫0∞e−4τdτ=2 V, so 2 V is the tightest bound.
No conflict. Causality concerns where h lives (t≥0) and stability concerns its absolute area (0.25). Here both hold, but each must be checked separately.
Physical meaning. The system is a first-order lag with time constant 0.25 s and DC gain 0.25. However the input moves within ±8 V, the output can never leave ±2 V.

answer.text: Test with a changing input. Let x(t)=8u(t)−16u(t−1): +8 V for 1 s, then −8 V for ever. It is bounded by 8 V. With s(t)=0.25(1−e−4t)u(t), y=8s(t)−16s(t−1):

answer: The output swings towards +2 V and then towards −2 V but never passes either, as the bound promised.

Mistakes that cost marks. Dropping the absolute value is harmless here only because h≥0. Quoting the bound as Mx·h(0)=8 V confuses the peak of h with its area. Claiming that because the system is causal it must be stable, or the reverse: each property needs its own test.

Sketch. h(t) starts at 1 at t=0 and falls to 0.018 by t=1 s (e−4); the shaded area under it is 0.25. The step response climbs from 0 to 0.25 with time constant 0.25 s, reaching 0.158 at t=0.25 s (63.2% of 0.25).
Closing check. The step input u(t) gives s(t)=0.25(1−e−4t)u(t), which settles at 0.25 V for a 1 V step: equal to the area, as the DC gain must be.

bank.q: Convert d²y/dt²+5dy/dt+6y=du/dt+2u (input u(t), output y(t)) into state equations in normal form. Define the state variables clearly and check the model.
outline: Why x₂=dy/dt fails when u′ appears
Check: characteristic roots and a step response
answer: Identify the coefficients. Compare with y″+a₁y′+a₀y=b₁u′+b₀u: a₁=5, a₀=6, b₁=1, b₀=2. The input is called u because x will name the states.
Why the plain choice fails. With x₁=y and x₂=y′, x₂′=y″=−6x₁−5x₂+u′+2u. This contains u′, so it is not of the form x′=Ax+Bu.
State choice. Take x₁=y and x₂=y′−b₁u=y′−u. Then y′=x₂+u.
First equation. x₁′=y′=x₂+u.

answer.text: Second equation. Differentiate x₂ and substitute y″ from the given equation:

answer: The u′ terms cancel, which is why this state was chosen. In general the coefficient of u is b₀−a₁b₁=2−5×1=−3.

answer.text: Normal form.

answer: So A=[0 1; −6 −5], B=[1; −3], C=[1 0], D=0. The state variables are x₁=y (the output) and x₂=y′−u (the output's slope minus the input).
Check 1: characteristic roots. det(λI−A)=λ(λ+5)+6=λ²+5λ+6=(λ+2)(λ+3). The roots −2 and −3 are those of the original equation, so A carries the right dynamics.

answer.text: Check 2: input-output relation. The right side u′+2u and the left side share the factor (D+2), with D=d/dt, so the system behaves as y′+3y=u. Its step response from rest is y(t)=(1/3)(1−e−3t). Simulating the state model with Euler steps of 1 ms for a unit step from x=0:

answer: General rule. For y″+a₁y′+a₀y=b₁u′+b₀u, the choice x₂=y′−b₁u always gives x₁′=x₂+b₁u and x₂′=−a₀x₁−a₁x₂+(b₀−a₁b₁)u. Here b₁=1, b₀=2, a₁=5, a₀=6, so B=[1; 2−5]=[1; −3], as derived.
Initial conditions in the new states. x₁(0)=y(0) and x₂(0)=y′(0)−u(0). From rest with u switched on at t=0+, the state starts at x=[0; 0].

Block diagram. Two integrators in a chain give x₂ and x₁. The input enters twice: with gain 1 directly into the derivative of x₁, and with gain −3 into the derivative of x₂. The feedback gains −6 (from x₁) and −5 (from x₂) enter the second summing point.

answer.text: The state choice is not unique. Another valid model: let z satisfy z″+5z′+6z=u, and take y=z′+2z (this reproduces u′+2u on the right). With x₁=z, x₂=z′:

answer: Same A, same roots, same input-output behaviour, different B and C. Examiners accept any valid choice if the states are defined clearly and the matrices match them.
Mistakes that cost marks. Leaving u′ inside x₂′; writing the last row of A as [6 5] instead of [−6 −5]; taking C=[1 0] in the second model, where the output is z′+2z, not z.
Closing check. The two columns agree to within 0.0001, the size of the Euler error, and the final value approaches 1/3=0.333, the DC gain b₀/a₀=2/6. The state model is correct.

bank.q: Compare two LTI systems with h₁(t)=δ(t−1) and h₂(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t). Discuss causality, BIBO stability, memory, and the output when the input is u(t).
outline: h₁: causal and stable; a pure 1 s delay
h₂: causal and stable; a first-order low-pass
Memory: h₁ remembers one instant, h₂ the whole past with fading weight
answer: Causality. h₁=δ(t−1) is zero except at t=1 s, so it is zero for t<0: causal. h₂=e−tu(t) is zero for t<0: causal.
BIBO stability. ∫|h₁|dt=∫δ(t−1)dt=1, finite: stable. ∫|h₂|dt=∫0∞e−tdt=1, finite: stable. Both have absolute area 1, so an input bounded by M gives an output bounded by M in both cases.

answer.text: Input-output rules. By the identity and shift property of convolution:
answer.pre:
System 1:  y₁(t) = x(t) * δ(t−1) = x(t − 1)                  (pure delay)
System 2:  y₂(t) = ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−τ</sup> x(t − τ) dτ                   (weighted past)

answer: Memory. A memoryless system has h(t)=Kδ(t). h₁ is not of that form: the output at t equals the input at t−1, so it has memory, but only of one past instant. h₂ uses every past input value, weighted by e−τ: an input 1 s old counts 0.368 as much as the present one, 3 s old only 0.050. Its memory is infinite but fading.

answer.text: Step responses. For x=u(t): y₁(t)=u(t−1), and y₂(t)=s₂(t)=∫0te−τdτ=(1−e−t)u(t).

answer: Shapes compared. System 1 copies the step exactly, 1 s late: it passes all frequencies unchanged (an ideal delay line). System 2 responds at once but rounds the edge, rising with time constant 1 s: a first-order low-pass filter like an RC circuit with RC=1 s.

answer.text: Cascade. By the associative law, the two in series have h=h₁*h₂=e−(t−1)u(t−1): the low-pass response delayed by 1 s. Its step response is (1−e−(t−1))u(t−1), which at t=2 s is 0.632.
answer.pre: h₁ * h₂ = δ(t−1) * e<sup>−t</sup>u(t) = e<sup>−(t−1)</sup> u(t−1)

answer: Summary. Both systems are causal, stable and have memory; they differ in how they use the past: one exact instant against an exponentially weighted history.
Memory length of system 2. The weight e−τ falls to 5% at τ=3 s, so in practice system 2 remembers about the last 3 seconds. System 1 remembers exactly the input 1 s ago and nothing else.

Response to a short pulse. A pulse of width 0.1 s and height 10 (area 1) comes out of system 1 unchanged, 1 s later. System 2 smears it into a curve close to e−tu(t), height about 1: it cannot reproduce sharp detail, which is what a low-pass filter does.
Real devices. A long cable behaves roughly like system 1 (it delays the signal); an RC circuit with RC=1 s is system 2. A real cable also smooths, so it is closer to the cascade of the two.

Mistakes that cost marks. Calling the delay "memoryless" because its impulse response is a single impulse: memoryless needs that impulse at t=0. Calling h₂ unstable because it never reaches zero: decaying forever is fine if the area is finite (here 1). Writing the cascade as e−tu(t−1) instead of e−(t−1)u(t−1).
Closing check. Both final values equal the areas of the impulse responses: y₁(∞)=1 and y₂(∞)=1, matching ∫h₁=∫h₂=1.

bank.q: For the system d²y/dt²+3dy/dt+2y=x(t), discuss the natural and forced responses. Relate the impulse response to the characteristic roots.
outline: Forced response for a step input
answer: Characteristic equation. Set x=0 and try y=eλt: λ²+3λ+2=0, so (λ+1)(λ+2)=0 and λ=−1, −2 s−1. Both roots are real and negative: two decaying modes, time constants 1 s and 0.5 s.
Natural response. yn(t)=c₁e−t+c₂e−2t, with c₁ and c₂ fixed by the two initial conditions y(0) and y′(0) after the forced part is added.
Forced response for a unit step. For t>0, x=1. Try a constant yf=K: 0+0+2K=1, so K=1/2. The total is y=c₁e−t+c₂e−2t+1/2.

answer.text: Step response from rest. y(0)=0 and y′(0)=0:
answer.pre:
c₁ + c₂ + 1/2 = 0
−c₁ − 2c₂ = 0        →   c₁ = −1,  c₂ = 1/2
s(t) = (1/2 − e<sup>−t</sup> + ½e<sup>−2t</sup>) u(t)

answer.text: Impulse response from the roots. For t>0 the input δ(t) is zero, so h is a pure natural response h=c₁e−t+c₂e−2t. Integrating the equation across t=0 shows that the impulse makes y′ jump by 1 while y stays continuous: y(0+)=0 and y′(0+)=1.
answer.pre:
c₁ + c₂ = 0
−c₁ − 2c₂ = 1        →   c₁ = 1,  c₂ = −1
h(t) = (e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>) u(t)

answer: The link. The impulse response is a sum of the characteristic modes, one term per root. Roots with negative real parts make every mode decay, so h is absolutely integrable (area 1−1/2=1/2) and the system is stable. A positive root would give a growing mode and an unstable system.
Consistency. ds/dt=e−t−e−2t=h(t) ✓, and s(∞)=1/2 equals the area of h.

answer.text: Zero-input and zero-state. Suppose instead y(0)=1, y′(0)=0 and x=0. Then c₁+c₂=1 and −c₁−2c₂=0 give c₁=2, c₂=−1: yzi=2e−t−e−2t. With a unit step as well, the total is yzi+s(t).

answer: Natural against zero-input. For the step from y(0)=1, y′(0)=0 the natural part has constants fitted to the total, so it is not the same as yzi; the forced part 1/2 is not the same as s(t). Both splits give the same total.

answer.text: Why y′ jumps by 1. Integrate the equation with x=δ(t) from 0− to 0+. The terms 3y′ and 2y integrate to zero if y is continuous, leaving
answer.pre: y′(0<sup>+</sup>) − y′(0<sup>−</sup>) = ∫ δ(t) dt = 1

answer: For a second-order equation with only x on the right, the impulse goes into the highest derivative: y″ contains δ, y′ jumps, and y stays continuous.

answer.text: Check h in the equation for t>0.
answer.pre:
h  = e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>
h′ = −e<sup>−t</sup> + 2e<sup>−2t</sup>
h″ = e<sup>−t</sup> − 4e<sup>−2t</sup>
h″ + 3h′ + 2h = (1 − 3 + 2)e<sup>−t</sup> + (−4 + 6 − 2)e<sup>−2t</sup> = 0   ✓

answer: Mistakes that cost marks. Setting y(0+)=1 and y′(0+)=0 for the impulse response gives h=2e−t−e−2t, which is the zero-input response of the table, not h. Using the forced value 1/2 when finding h (the input is zero for t>0, so there is no forced part). Mixing the constants of the natural/forced split with those of the zero-input/zero-state split.
Closing check. h peaks where h′=−e−t+2e−2t=0, that is e−t=1/2, t=ln 2=0.693 s, with h=0.5−0.25=0.25, matching the table.

bank.q: Explain the graphical evaluation of the convolution integral. Use x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2) and h(t)=u(t)−u(t−1) to obtain y(t), and comment on its duration and shape.
outline: Find the overlap intervals and breakpoints
Trapezoid shape; duration is the sum of the widths; area check
answer: The integral. y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ over all τ. For each output time t, the output is the area under the product of x(τ) and the flipped, shifted h.

answer.text: The routine.
answer.pre:
1. Sketch x(τ) on a τ axis.
2. Flip h(τ) about τ = 0 to get h(−τ).
3. Slide it right by t to get h(t − τ).
4. Multiply x(τ) h(t − τ) at every τ.
5. Integrate over the overlap; repeat for every range of t.

answer: The signals. x(τ)=1 on 0≤τ<2 (a 2 s unit pulse). h(τ)=1 on 0≤τ<1. After flipping and sliding, h(t−τ)=1 on t−1<τ≤t: a 1 s window whose right edge is at τ=t.
Breakpoints. The window's right edge reaches the pulse at t=0; its left edge enters at t=1; its right edge leaves at t=2; its left edge leaves at t=3. These give five ranges.

answer.text: Overlap in each range. Both heights are 1, so y(t) equals the length of the overlap.
Picture at t=1.5 s. The 1 s window sits fully inside the pulse, from τ=0.5 to τ=1.5, so y(1.5)=1. The lower plot joins the results of every range.

svg.aria: Top: the pulse x of width 2 and the flipped pulse h of width 1 placed at t equals 1.5 s, overlapping from 0.5 to 1.5. Bottom: y(t) rises as t to 1 at t=1, stays at 1 until t=2 and falls as 3 minus t to zero at t=3.

answer: Continuity. At t=1, t=1 and 1 agree; at t=2, 1 and 3−2=1 agree; at t=3, 3−3=0. No jumps, as expected for two signals without impulses.

Shape. y(t) is a trapezoid: a ramp up while the short pulse enters, a flat top of height 1 while it is fully inside the long pulse, and a ramp down while it leaves. The flat top lasts Tx−Th=2−1=1 s. If the widths were equal the flat top would shrink to a point and y would be a triangle.
Duration. y is nonzero from 0+0=0 to 2+1=3 s, a width of 3 s=Tx+Th. This is the width rule from the properties of convolution.
Peak. AxAh·min(Tx, Th)=1×1×1=1, as found.

Evaluation of the method. The graphical method is reliable because it shows where the limits change; the most common error, using 0 to t for every t, would give y=t for all t≥0, which grows without bound and contradicts the finite width 3 s that the width rule demands.

answer.text: The integrals in each range.
answer.pre:
0 ≤ t < 1:  y = ∫₀ᵗ 1·1 dτ = t
1 ≤ t < 2:  y = ∫ from t−1 to t of 1 dτ = 1
2 ≤ t < 3:  y = ∫ from t−1 to 2 of 1 dτ = 2 − (t − 1) = 3 − t

answer.text: Cross-check with ramps. x=u(t)−u(t−2) and h=u(t)−u(t−1). With r(t)=t·u(t)=u*u and the distributive and shift laws:

answer: Smoothing. The input has sharp edges; the output has ramps instead. Convolving with a 1 s pulse is a 1 s moving average (times 1 s), which rounds every edge over 1 s. This is how a simple averaging filter smooths a noisy signal.

answer: When to use which method. The graphical method is fastest for pulses and piecewise signals with few breakpoints; the analytic integral is better for exponentials; the ramp decomposition is the quickest check. A full answer uses one method and checks with another.
Closing check. The area of y must be area(x)×area(h)=2×1=2. Trapezoid area=½(3+1)×1=2. ✓

bank.q: A student claims: "Every causal LTI system is BIBO stable." Evaluate the claim. Either prove it or give a counterexample using h(t), and state the correct relation between causality and stability.
answer: What each property says. Causality: h(t)=0 for t<0. BIBO stability: ∫|h(t)|dt<∞. The first is about the time support of h, the second about its absolute area. Nothing in the first limits the second.
Counterexample. Take h(t)=u(t), the ideal integrator y(t)=∫−∞tx(τ)dτ. It is zero for t<0, so it is causal.
Absolute area. ∫|u(t)|dt=∫0∞1 dt grows without limit, so the stability condition fails.

answer.text: A bounded input with an unbounded output. Apply x(t)=u(t), bounded by 1:
answer.pre: y(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 1 dτ = t,   t ≥ 0

answer: The output is the ramp t·u(t): 10 at t=10 s, 1000 at t=1000 s. No finite bound exists, so the system is not BIBO stable. The claim is false.
A second counterexample. h(t)=etu(t) is causal; its area ∫0∞etdt is infinite, and the step input gives y=(et−1)u(t), which is 1.72 at 1 s and 22,025 at 10 s.

answer.text: The converse is false too. h(t)=e2tu(−t) is noncausal but has area 1/2, so it is stable.

answer: Correct relation. Causality and BIBO stability are independent properties of an LTI system. Causality ⇔ h(t)=0 for t<0. BIBO stability ⇔ ∫|h(t)|dt<∞. Both must be tested on h(t) separately, and all four combinations occur.

Where the student's idea comes from. Many familiar causal systems (RC filters, damped springs) are also stable, so it is tempting to link the two. But stability in those systems comes from energy loss (resistance, damping), not from causality.

Physical counterexample. A capacitor charged by a current source: v(t)=(1/C)∫i dt. It is causal, and a constant current of 1 mA into 1 μF raises the voltage by 1 V every millisecond without limit, until the capacitor breaks down. Its impulse response (1/C)u(t) is not absolutely integrable.

The correct statement for exponential systems. For a causal h(t) made of terms c·eλtu(t), each term has finite area only if its λ is negative (or has a negative real part). So a causal system of this kind is stable exactly when every λ has a negative real part; Laplace transform analysis restates this as all poles in the left half of the s-plane. Causality alone says nothing about the signs of the λs.
Verdict. The claim is false; the correct relation is independence, with both conditions checked on h(t).
Closing check. For the stable causal case e−tu(t) the same step input gives y=1−e−t, bounded by 1 = area of h, so the bound Mx·∫|h| holds there and fails only where the area is infinite.

glossary.def: A system that is both linear and time-invariant.
The property that a system obeys superposition: scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs.
The output for x₁+x₂ equals the output for x₁ plus the output for x₂.
The output for a·x(t) equals a times the output for x(t), for any constant a.
A delay of the input by t₀ produces the same output delayed by t₀; also called shift invariance.
A generalised signal that is zero for t≠0, has unit area and picks out a value under an integral: ∫x(τ)δ(t−τ)dτ=x(t).
A signal equal to 1 for t≥0 and 0 for t<0; its derivative is δ(t).
The output of an LTI system for input δ(t), starting at rest.
The output of an LTI system for input u(t), starting at rest; also called the indicial response.
The operation y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ that gives the output of an LTI system.
The integration variable τ in the convolution integral; it disappears once the integral is evaluated.
A value of t at which an edge of h(t−τ) crosses an edge of x(τ), so the limits of the convolution integral change.
Systems connected in series; for LTI systems the overall impulse response is h₁*h₂.
A system whose impulse response satisfies h*h<sub>inv</sub>=δ, so it undoes the first system; using it is called deconvolution.
A system whose output never depends on future input; for an LTI system, h(t)=0 for t<0.
Every bounded input produces a bounded output; for an LTI system, ∫|h(t)|dt<∞.
A signal with finite area under its absolute value, ∫|h(t)|dt<∞.
A system whose output depends only on the present input; for an LTI system, h(t)=Kδ(t).
Linear constant-coefficient differential equation: a weighted sum of y and its derivatives equals a weighted sum of x and its derivatives, with constant weights.
The polynomial equation in λ obtained by trying y=e<sup>λt</sup> in the equation with zero input; its roots give the natural modes.
τ=RC for an RC circuit or L/R for an RL circuit; the first-order step response reaches 63.2% of its final value at t=τ.
The part of the solution that solves the equation with zero input, built from the characteristic modes.
A particular solution with the shape of the input, such as a constant for a step input.
The output due to stored energy (initial conditions) alone, with the input set to zero.
The output due to the input alone, with the system starting at rest; it equals x*h.
One of a set of signals whose values at one instant, with the future input, fix the system's future behaviour.
The first-order matrix equation x′=Ax+Bu that updates the state vector.
A system written as n first-order equations, each solved for the derivative of one state variable.
The phase-variable state model whose A matrix has 1s above the diagonal and the negated equation coefficients in its last row.
